Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.

items.title: Non-Myopic Safety Filtering with Learned Intervention Cost-to-Go
items.summary: Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters minimize instantaneous deviation from a nominal control command, but a sequence of pointwise-minimal interventions need not minimize cumulative intervention effort. This paper proposes a discrete-time non-myopic safety filter using a learned approximation of the optimal intervention cost-to-go over CBF-admissible policies. The approximation enters through a relaxed Bellman-residual constraint, while the original barrier condition remains hard. Feasibility is equivalent to that of the conventional CBF filter, and forward invariance remains independent of approximation accuracy under the stated assumptions. We derive a trajectory-wise performance certificate that requires neither the optimal value function nor an approximation-error bound. Under additional approximation and horizon assumptions, a suboptimality bound contains an explicit endpoint approximation-error term together with accumulated tolerance and relaxation terms. Numerical results for a collision-avoidance problem show an approximately 50% reduction in mean cumulative intervention effort relative to conventional CBF filtering over 100 initial conditions not used during training or parameter selection. The improvement is consistent across three independently trained networks, while maintaining the prescribed safety constraints and requiring less online computation than the tested predictive filter.

items.title: Limited-Memory First-Order Methods: Identification, Reconstruction, $H$-Duality and Application to Optimized Methods
items.summary: In general, linear-span first-order methods add at every iteration a combination of all observed gradients to the previous iterate. However, many methods of interest can be implemented in a way that requires storing only a few auxiliary vectors, instead of all past gradients. We call such methods limited-memory first-order methods. A given fixed-coefficient first-order method can be described by a lower triangular coefficient matrix, which expresses each step as a combination of previous gradients. We show that the minimum number of running sums required to implement a method is equal to the minimum rank of a completion of the strict lower triangular part of its coefficient matrix, and propose a reconstruction algorithm. Moreover, taking the $H$-dual of a method, which reflects the coefficient matrix across its anti-diagonal, preserves its memory and translates into a permutation and time-reversal on the coefficients of the running sum recurrences. We apply our results to two optimized first-order methods for smooth strongly convex functions. First, our reconstruction applied to a method numerically designed by Shu and Wang reveals a recurrence with one auxiliary vector, which is related to the Triple Momentum Method (TMM) of Van Scoy, Freeman and Lynch with a particular initialization. We prove that the reconstructed method, called TMM-GD, is minimax optimal at every horizon for the final distance to the minimizer relative to the initial gradient norm. Second, the Information-Theoretic Exact Method (ITEM) of Taylor and Drori, optimal for the final distance relative to the initial one, is known to be memory one. We give an explicit recurrence with one auxiliary vector for its $H$-dual, called ITEM-GG, and prove that ITEM-GG is the unique minimax optimal nonadaptive linear-span method for the final gradient norm relative to the initial one.

items.title: Trustworthy Numerical Software in the Age of AI: What Would Turing Do?
items.summary: AI coding agents can now produce numerical software faster than human experts can review it, raising serious concerns about usability and reliability. These and other AI tools are already transforming mathematics and software, and they will soon transform mathematical software. These concerns motivated us to assess AI-generated numerical linear algebra (NLA) kernels, which we did through an audit of a recent public GPU QR competition. All five leading kernels passed the competition's accuracy tests, and the winning kernel achieved a 107-fold speedup over the competition's baseline, which calls NVIDIA's QR routine. Yet each failed at least once on new inputs, even those from the competition's generator, under the same checker, while the baseline passed them all. In light of this, we want to develop reusable formalizations of numerical analysis methods, which remain sparsely represented in existing formal libraries. We describe VSCL, our Lean library of mathematical foundations for numerical computing. We also propose VERNA to connect these tasks by using formalized results to guide kernel assessment against explicit specifications. Drawing on Turing's work on rounding-error analysis and program checking, we discuss design principles for developing trustworthy numerical software when direct human checking is impractical.

items.title: Second scaling regime in high-dimensional function approximation and curse of dimensionality
items.summary: High-dimensional function approximation is often subject to the curse of dimensionality, commonly described by a hypercube scaling regime with a large expense of $R^d$ grid points, where $R$ denotes the side length of a hypercube in $d$ dimensions. Here we show that a second scaling regime, which we call the lattice ball scaling regime, also arises and is relevant for practical applications. In this regime, the expense scales as $d^{R^2}/(R^2!)$ and therefore grows polynomially with $d$. This regime arises without additional special assumptions of special types of function spaces or error norms. The lattice ball scaling regime occurs when $R^2\ll d$, due to the discrete nature of counting the expense as the number of lattice points inside a hypersphere. Here we investigate this regime, which arises from the classical problem of approximating high-dimensional functions from common spaces of analytic or $m$-times continuously differentiable functions using orthogonal series (spectral method) such as Fourier, Chebyshev, and Legendre polynomial series. For many applications, the expense in the lattice ball scaling regime can be substantially smaller than that of the hypercube scaling regime, making accurate approximations more accessible. Numerical illustrations include classifying images of handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset and learning the solution operators of partial differential equations, such as Burgers' equation and the radiative transfer equation. The potential for connections with artificial neural networks and other machine learning methods is also discussed.

items.title: Fundamental Tradeoffs in Sampling, Transmission and Information Freshness: Instantaneous Feedback
items.summary: We study a time-slotted generate-at-will status-update system over an erasure channel with transmission success probability $q$, subject to average sampling- and transmission-rate constraints $f_s$ and $f_r$, respectively. The sampler-transmitter pair jointly decides whether to idle, retransmit a stale packet, or replace it with a fresh sample. We derive a universal lower bound on the optimal average age of information, analyze a class of stationary randomized policies, and obtain an optimal policy within this class that provides a $4$-approximation guarantee. The joint problem reduces to the sampling-constrained problem when $f_s\leq qf_r$ and the transmission-constrained problem when $f_s\geq f_r$. For $qf_r<f_s<f_r$, we formulate a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) and introduce the class $\barΠ$ of $(W,R)$ policies, where $W$ specifies a waiting threshold for transmission and $R$ specifies a packet-replacement threshold. We prove that, for every choice of Lagrange multipliers, the corresponding Lagrangian-relaxed Markov decision process admits an optimal policy in $\barΠ$. We then formulate a linear program (LP) over distributions of $(W,R)$ policies and prove that choosing a policy according to an optimal LP solution yields an optimal CMDP policy. Moreover, there exists an optimal LP solution assigning positive probability to at most three $(W,R)$ policies. Since $\barΠ$ is countably infinite, for every $ε>0$ we construct a finite subset $\barΠ_ε\subset\barΠ$ and show that the LP restricted to this set yields an $ε$-optimal policy. Finally, we derive a stronger pair of lower bounds by considering systems with only the sampling-rate or transmission-rate constraint. Using these bounds, we construct a policy randomizing among four $(W,R)$ policies with a $2$-approximation guarantee for $qf_r<f_s<f_r$.

items.title: The Sum of Leaf Weights in the Minimum Spanning Tree of the Complete Graph
items.summary: Let $G_n$ be a random weighted complete graph on $n$ vertices, where edges have i.i.d. $\text{Unif}(0,1)$ weights. Let $T_n$ be the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of $G_n$. The expected weight of $T_n$ is known to converge to $ζ(3) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^3}$ (Frieze 1985). We investigate the sum of weights of edges incident to the leaves of $T_n$, denoting this quantity by $L_n$. We give tight upper and lower bounds on $\mathbb{E}[L_n]$ and determine its limit as $n$ diverges, leveraging typical behavior of sparse Erdős--Rényi random graphs. We also establish concentration of $L_n$ around $\mathbb{E}[L_n]$ and almost sure convergence to this value. These results directly yield substantial improvements to state-of-the-art bounds for two important variants of the MST problem: (1) an improved upper bound on the weight of the optimal random instance Steiner tree, as studied by Bollobás, Gamarnik, Riordan, and Sudakov (2004); and (2) an improvement over the upper bound for the Probabilistic Minimum Spanning Tree, introduced by Bertsimas (1988).

items.title: A Scalable Decentralized Event-Triggered Topology-Switching Protocol for Verifiable Safety in Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: This paper develops a decentralized event-triggered topology-switching protocol that allows agents to disconnect from the communication network while preserving state safety and excluding Zeno behavior. We establish a robust barrier function condition that guarantees safety as long as the estimation error remains within a prescribed threshold. Each agent uses locally computable certificates to determine when to connect and disconnect from the network. The certificate construction improves scalability by reducing the complexity of topology-dependent computations from $O(2^N)$ to $O(N)$, where $N$ is the number of agents. We formally prove that the protocol ensures the estimation error does not exceed the prescribed threshold and is non-Zeno. An alternating method computes an error-weighting matrix and a quadratic barrier function that guarantee safety under the proposed protocol. Finally, we evaluate the protocol on four interconnected microgrids. Compared with maintaining network connectivity at all times, the protocol reduces the time agents remain connected while keeping phase and frequency within their safe operating region.

items.title: Exponential Quantum Memory Advantage for Late-Graph Smoothness and Spectral Estimation
items.summary: Graph signal processing tests how smoothly the decisions of next-generation massive sensor networks with $N$ nodes vary over their neighbour graph. Memory becomes the bottleneck when the neighbour graph arrives only after data erasure, a late-graph setting motivated by dispersed sensor networks and telemetry. We analyse three collection scenarios, reliable rounds, continuous broadcast and ordered capture, and test the Dirichlet energy $\mathcal E_G=\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf L\mathbf z/N$ of the fused decision map $\mathbf z\in\{\pm1\}^N$, with late-graph Laplacian $\mathbf L$, against two thresholds. Hidden Matching uses $O(\log N)$ qubits on fused bits, but in reliable rounds and continuous broadcast, where nodes report $b$ sub-bits separately, a classical record buffer before it uses $O(N b)$ bits; classical methods need $Ω(\sqrt N)$ bits in the worst case. The recently introduced Quantum Oracle Sketching builds quantum oracles from random data streams without storing them. We combine coherent loading of separately reported sub-bits, exact in reliable rounds and by Quantum Oracle Sketching in continuous broadcast, with nonlinear fusion and Hidden Matching readout. The register count $R$ does not grow with $N$, and the memory is $O(\log N)$ logical qubits and classical bits, at fixed $b$, graph bounds, thresholds and error targets: an exponential memory advantage over every classical receiver and over Hidden Matching with that buffer. We prove unbiasedness in reliable rounds, preparation bounds in continuous broadcast, classical lower bounds and, for a planner-supplied multi-hop coefficient stream, spectral error bounds. Broadcast simulations match analytic averages at $N=1024$, without resolved bias growth up to $N=2^{20}$. Fault-tolerant hardware, gate rates and, in continuous broadcast, report counts remain open.

items.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Maximum Witness Set
items.summary: A witness set in a polygon is a set of points whose visibility regions are pairwise disjoint. Since no point of the polygon can see more than one witness, the cardinality of a witness set provides a lower bound on the minimum number of guards required to cover the polygon. Finding a maximum witness set is therefore a natural packing counterpart to the classical Art Gallery problem. While the latter is $\exists\mathbb{R}$-complete, the computational complexity of finding a maximum witness set in a general simple polygon has remained open. In this paper, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for computing a maximum witness set in a simple polygon with $n$ vertices, of which $ρ$ are reflex, assuming that no three vertices are collinear. Our algorithm runs in $\mathcal{O}(ρ^4n^6\log n)$ time. Our approach exploits a tree structure induced by witness visibility regions and employs geometric dynamic programming over nested regions determined by visibility windows.

items.title: Reducing Asymmetric Path TSP to Asymmetric TSP
items.summary: In the Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem (Asymmetric TSP), we are given distances between $n$ vertices that satisfy the triangle inequality but need not be symmetric, and we seek a shortest tour through all vertices. In its path version, Asymmetric Path TSP, two vertices $s$ and $t$ are prescribed, and we seek a shortest path from $s$ to $t$ through all vertices. Both problems are equivalent to their versions with arbitrary nonnegative edge costs on a directed graph, in which vertices may be visited more than once. We show that for all constants $α\ge1$ and $\varepsilon>0$, any $α$-approximation algorithm for Asymmetric TSP yields an $(α+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for Asymmetric Path TSP. The best previous reduction of this kind, due to Feige and Singh, yields an $α(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm. Our result answers an open question of Traub and Vygen. Consequently, every constant-factor approximation guarantee for Asymmetric TSP carries over to Asymmetric Path TSP up to an arbitrarily small additive error.

items.title: Bregman primal-dual methods for conic linear optimization via exact-penalty and self-dual formulations
items.summary: We study Bregman primal--dual proximal methods for conic linear programs (LPs). For problems involving non-polyhedral cones, Bregman distances lead to generalized projections that are often simpler than Euclidean projections. In this paper, we reformulate conic LPs as equivalent exact-penalty problems over truncated cones, and use self-dual embeddings to construct such formulations systematically. This approach yields Bregman proximal methods with simpler subproblems and convergence guarantees over bounded domains. We also study line searches for the Bregman primal--dual hybrid gradient and extragradient methods applied to self-dual problems. For logarithmically homogeneous kernels, the Bregman distances from the starting points are unbounded on the truncated cone, and the classical ergodic bounds do not apply. For these kernels, we derive convergence rates for the exact-penalty objective at the averaged iterates of both methods. Numerical experiments with nonnegative trigonometric polynomial optimization and sparse semidefinite optimization indicate the potential of this framework as a general-purpose approach for incorporating efficient Bregman projections in conic linear optimization.

items.title: Vanishing Relative Distance of Uniformly Random CSS LDPC Codes Built from Permutation Matrices
items.summary: Classical random regular low-density parity-check codes can have minimum distance growing linearly with block length. We study CSS check matrices formed as full $J\times L$ arrays of arbitrary $P\times P$ permutation matrices, sampled uniformly subject to commutation. For fixed column weight $J\ge3$ and fixed even row weight $L>2J$, we prove that the relative minimum distance converges to zero in probability as $P\to\infty$, with block length $n=LP$. We analyze the weight enumerators that count all nontrivial logical representatives after excluding stabilizers. A coefficientwise lower bound shows that, at every fixed relative weight $0<α<1$ along even-weight sequences, exponentially many such representatives exist with high probability. Their typical and mean counts have exponent lower bound $h_2(α)/2$, where $h_2$ is the binary entropy function. We compare this bound with the classical LDPC and dense CSS mean weight-distribution exponents. The existence, with high probability, of a logical operator below every fixed target weight $δn$ yields the distance conclusion.

items.title: Douglas--Rachford Algorithm with Relaxed Resolvents
items.summary: The Douglas--Rachford algorithm is a classical method for finding a zero of the sum of two maximally monotone operators. In its standard form, both operators are reflected in the same manner and are activated with the same step-size. In this article we break this symmetry by replacing the reflected resolvents by relaxed resolvents, letting the two operators be activated with different step-sizes. We show that this additional freedom is available precisely when the operators are cocoercive, the admissible range of the parameter being determined by their cocoercivity constants and reducing to the classical algorithm when these constants vanish. Within this range we quantify the averagedness of the resulting operator, which yields the weak convergence of the method together with relaxation steps beyond those allowed in the classical case, and, when one of the operators is in addition strongly monotone, a strict contraction. We compute in closed form the parameters minimizing the contraction factor and we exhibit instances attaining it, so that the resulting linear rates are tight. The optimal rates are strictly smaller than the best rates available for the classical Douglas--Rachford algorithm in the monotone inclusion and convex optimization settings, which are studied separately. All theoretical rates are corroborated by the numerical worst cases obtained via performance estimation.

items.title: tsspiral: An R Package to Create Circular Versions of Time Series Plots
items.summary: `tsspiral` is an open-source R package that introduces a circular approach to time series visualisation using polar coordinates. We refer to this circular representation of time series data as a spiral. `tsspiral` provides a collection of `ggplot2` geometries for creating a spiral representation of time series data. In our approach, we arrange observations around a circle. Each year is represented by a circle, with the angular position corresponding to the day of the year, and successive years appear as concentric rings. This arrangement facilitates the exploration of periodicity, seasonality, and recurring temporal patterns, particularly in long time series. The package also supports temporal hierarchical visualisations to compare patterns across time scales. By bringing polar-coordinate-based visualisation into routine time series analysis, `tsspiral` offers a practical tool for exploring temporal patterns and communicating complex time-dependent structures. Rather than treating spiral plots as standalone graphics, our approach brings them into the grammar of graphics framework, enabling users to explore temporal patterns through a broader range of visual encodings.

items.title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions
items.summary: This paper presents a computational model integrating transmural drug transport, smooth muscle cell contraction, nonlinear anisotropic material behavior, and residual stresses to investigate the effects of calcium channel blockers~(CCBs) on local stress distributions in atherosclerotic arteries. The balance of linear momentum is coupled with a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for the drug transport. Smooth muscle contraction is modeled phenomenologically based on a chemo-mechanical model that incorporates the effects of stretch on intracellular calcium dynamics and calcium sensitization. A novel drug-tissue interaction model is proposed to capture the effects of CCBs on intracellular calcium and thus on smooth muscle contraction. Material parameters are identified by fitting to experimental data from the literature and finite element simulations are conducted on five exemplary atherosclerotic arterial geometries reconstructed from histological cross-sections. Simulation results show that although CCBs reduce the stresses in the media through reduced smooth muscle contraction, they shift load to the fibrous cap, whose stress increases in all five geometries (median of up to 28.9~kPa). This increase varies strongly between plaque morphologies and becomes smaller with lower smooth muscle tone before treatment, lower drug concentrations in the arterial wall and increasing axial pre-stretch. A blood pressure reduction of 10~mmHg already lowers it to a median of at most 3.8~kPa in four of the five geometries. Our findings suggest that CCBs may increase the rupture risk of vulnerable plaques with highly loaded fibrous caps under insufficient blood pressure reduction, which remains to be confirmed experimentally and clinically.

items.title: Constant-Factor Matching-Size Estimation in Random-Order Streams
items.summary: We give a one-pass algorithm that estimates the maximum matching size of an arbitrary simple graph within a constant factor using $O(\log^2 n)$ bits of space. The edges arrive exactly once in uniformly random order. The algorithm succeeds with probability at least $2/3$, does not require the number of edges in advance, and has worst-case total running time $O((m+1)\log(n+2))$ on a word RAM. Kapralov, Khanna, and Sudan (SODA 2014) obtained a polylogarithmic approximation in polylogarithmic space. Kapralov, Mitrović, Norouzi-Fard, and Tardos (SODA 2020) subsequently gave a constant-factor approximation from independent uniform edge samples and an $O(\log^2 n)$-approximation in random order. We obtain a constant factor in the latter model with the same $O(\log^2 n)$ space bound. The main ingredient is a comparison between the memory states of a recursive sampling algorithm under sampling with and without replacement. We account jointly for the sampled edges retained by the recursion and the positions at which they arrived. Randomized thresholds limit the additional information stored in numerical counters. A bound on the expected work of the entire recursion then removes the loss from its logarithmic depth. The resulting estimator repeatedly improves a coarse estimate while storing only one recursion stack.

items.title: Certified Nash Equilibrium Learning for Nonzero-Sum Jump-Diffusion Games: Policy Iteration and Off-Policy Q-Learning
items.summary: This paper establishes two model-free reinforcement learning methods for infinite-horizon N-player linear-quadratic nonzero-sum stochastic differential games whose drift, Brownian diffusion, and Poisson jump amplitudes depend on all players' controls. Control dependence in the diffusion and jump terms couples the players' simultaneous feedback updates. A verifiable certificate ensures that the partially model-free policy iteration map is contractive on an invariant closed ball centered at an admissible initial feedback profile. All feedback iterates are mean-square stabilizing, and the algorithm achieves local geometric convergence of feedback gains and value matrices to those associated with a closed-loop Nash equilibrium. The term certified refers to a verifiable convergence certificate that guarantees mean-square stability of all policy iterates and local geometric convergence to a closed-loop Nash equilibrium. To implement the policy updates from data, the off-policy Q-learning algorithm reuses the same behavior-policy data across iterations without requiring the system coefficients or jump intensity. Under quantitative persistence of excitation and a common initialization, exact population regression reproduces the policy-iteration sequence. The same local convergence guarantee therefore applies to off-policy Q-learning at the population level. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the two proposed algorithms.

items.title: Odd faces as a parameter for maximum independent set in embedded graphs
items.summary: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for finding a maximum weight independent set in a graph embedded in a surface of bounded genus and with a bounded number of vertex-disjoint odd faces. In particular, we obtain an algorithm for graphs with an even-faced embedding in a torus and for planar graphs with a bounded number of odd faces, answering a question of Thomassé (2018) and a question of Choi, Gorsky, Kim, McFarland, and Wiederrecht (2025) respectively. We reduce the original problem to finding a minimum cost non-negative integer circulation with homology constraints in the dual of a certain double cover of the original graph.

items.title: Recursive Spectral Graph Partitioning Coding for Index Assignment in Semantic Communications
items.summary: Transmitting quantized semantic embeddings over a bit-flip channel requires a binary mapping that minimizes expected reconstruction distortion. The classical Binary Switching Algorithm (BSA) ($\mathcal{O}(K^3 \log K)$ for $K$ centroids) yields locally optimal assignments but ignores hierarchical bit significance, making it incompatible with Unequal Error Protection (UEP). We propose Recursive Spectral Graph Partitioning (RSGP), which recursively bisects the centroid affinity graph along the Fiedler eigenvector so that early bits separate semantically distant groups while later bits refine local structure. RSGP runs in $\mathcal{O}(K^3)$ with no iterative outer loop, and is the only method studied to show a systematic positive UEP gain: protecting early bits over later ones improves accuracy for RSGP, while being neutral or harmful for unstructured assignments. Experiments on the Banking77 dataset and the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) confirm that RSGP consistently matches or exceeds BSA accuracy across codebook sizes and error profiles.

items.title: Simultaneous reconstruction of an obstacle and its wavenumber for the Helmholtz equation: a robust optimization approach
items.summary: In this paper, we propose a method to recover simultaneously the shape and wavenumber of an object from noisy radar or sonar measurements. The physical problem is modeled in a bounded domain with the Helmholtz equation and appropriate transmission conditions. The approach relies on a Kohn-Vogelius formulation of the inverse problem and uses Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent combined with shape optimization techniques. To address the robustness of the method with respect to measurement noise, we are looking to minimize a convex combination of the expected value and variance, which we achieve by using a Karhunen-Lo{è}ve expansion. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through twodimensional numerical experiments.

items.title: Full-Cover and Non-Overlapping Uni-domination in Graphs: Bounds and Complexity
items.summary: A vertex is uni-dominated by a set $S \subseteq V(G)$ if exactly one vertex of $S$ lies in its closed neighborhood, and the uni-domination number $\mathrm{ud}^*(G)$ is the largest number of vertices a single set can uni-dominate. The graphs admitting an efficient dominating set are those with $\mathrm{ud}^*(G) = n$. Hedetniemi and Rall asked for the largest constant $c$ with $\mathrm{ud}^*(T) \geq c \cdot n$ for every tree $T$ of order $n$. We answer their question: the constant is $4/5$, and a set attaining it can be computed in linear time. This set is moreover a dominating set. Recall that an efficient dominating set satisfies two requirements at once: it dominates every vertex, and it dominates no vertex twice. Our set satisfies the first one, which leads us to study $\mathrm{ud}^*$ under each of the two requirements separately, giving the Full-Cover variant $\mathrm{ud}^*_0$ and the Non-Overlapping variant $\mathrm{ud}^*_+$. The two behave very differently: on arbitrarily large graphs $\mathrm{ud}^*_0$ may remain bounded by a constant, whereas $\mathrm{ud}^*_+$ always grows with the order. We present bounds for both, and show that the associated decision problems are polynomial for constant thresholds and NP-complete for the thresholds $\lceil \sqrt[c]{n} \rceil$ and $4\sqrt{n}$, respectively, the latter even on split graphs. Finally, we show that neither of the two parameters bounds the other.

items.title: Linear Network Coding for Sum All-Reduce over Ring Networks
items.summary: Sum All-Reduce is a fundamental collective communication primitive in which each node holds a local vector and every node must recover the componentwise sum of all vectors. In distributed training, this operation is often implemented over a ring topology using a reduce--multicast scheme. We study sum All-Reduce on directed rings via linear network coding, which includes reduce--multicast as a special case. We give a necessary and sufficient feasibility condition in terms of the coding matrices. For a ring with $N\geq 3$ nodes and unit-capacity links, where each node holds a vector containing $K$ symbols, we prove that the number of time units $T$ required by any feasible linear code satisfies $T\ge\max\bigl\{K+N-2,\ \lceil\frac{2(N-1)}{N}K\rceil\bigr\}$, giving a rate $K/T$ of at most $N/(2(N-1))$. The bound is tight over every field. When $K\ge N$, an interleaved reduce--multicast code achieves the bound; when $K<N$ and $K$ divides $N$, a reduce--partial-multicast code does. When $K<N$ and $K$ does not divide $N$, no coordinate-wise code---in particular, no reduce--multicast code---achieves the bound, while an explicit linear network code does.

items.title: A Polynomial Time Algorithm for Finding a Minimum 5-Partition of a Submodular Function
items.summary: Given a real-valued submodular function on a finite ground set, the minimum $k$-partition problem asks for a partition into $k$ nonempty parts minimizing the sum of their function values. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for $k=5$. The idea follows directly from the previous $k=4$ result, where there is precisely one obstruction for generalizing it to $k=5$. We show the special case can be handled by reasoning about a restricted family of $3$-partitions.

items.title: An Optimal Online Algorithm for Single-machine Scheduling with Two Agents
items.summary: This paper addresses the online two-agent scheduling problem on a single machine, where jobs arrive over time. The objective is to minimize the weighted sum of the agents' makespans, denoted as $C_{\max}^A + θC_{\max}^B$, for a given priority weight $θ\ge 1$. A significant gap has persisted between the established theoretical lower bound on the competitive ratio and the performance of the best-known online algorithms. For the parameter range $1 \leq θ\leq \tfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$, we propose novel online algorithm which achieves a competitive ratio of $1+\tfracθ{1+θ}$. This result matches the theoretical lower bound.

items.title: Long-time asymptotics of advection-diffusion of finite element differential forms
items.summary: This paper establishes global numerical analysis for the long-time behavior of Lie advection--diffusion of differential forms discretized by finite element exterior calculus (FEEC). For potential flows we prove a weighted Hodge decomposition implying convergence to harmonic forms of dimension equal to the Betti number, yielding a differential-form antidynamo theorem. For general advection, a mixed FEEC scheme is introduced and shown to preserve key structural properties: the dimension of closed stationary discrete $k$-forms is at least $b_k$. Under verified spectral-preservation assumptions (satisfied for small $h$ by spectral approximation and for arbitrary $h$ by a lowest-order exponential-fitting $M$-matrix discretization), discrete antidynamo theorems are obtained. In particular, on two-dimensional manifolds the numerical $1$-forms converge exponentially to a uniquely determined closed stationary form for every diffusion coefficient $η>0$, rigorously excluding spurious dynamo growth. The results guarantee that FEEC faithfully inherits the topological long-time asymptotics of the continuous system.

items.title: Policy Iteration Convergence for Exploratory Two-State Mean-Field Control Problems
items.summary: This paper studies the theoretical policy iteration convergence for two-state mean-field control (MFC) problems with Wright--Fisher common noise under entropy regularization. The population dynamics lead to a degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation of Kimura type. After an arcsine transformation, the degeneracy becomes a singular Bessel drift whose coefficients and weights depend on the feedback stochastic policy. This policy dependence prevents a direct application of estimates for a fixed operator. We establish weighted Sobolev estimates and Hölder embeddings uniformly over the admissible policy class. Combining these estimates with logarithmic entropy bounds and boundary estimates that remain valid when the policy changes, we prove the well-posedness, monotone improvement and convergence of policy iteration to the optimal solution. We also establish the convergence to the original MFC problem when the entropy parameter $λ$ tends to zero. Both the regularization error and the performance loss of the regularized optimal policy are bounded by $O(λ(1+|\lnλ|))$ in a weighted Hölder norm. An epidemic containment example of MFC is presented to illustrate the policy iteration convergence and the vanishing entropy convergence.

items.title: Path-constrained Packing on Trees
items.summary: An instance of Budgeted Path-constrained Packing on Trees (BPPT) consists of a graph $G$ together with a spanning tree $T$, a weight $w_e \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ for each tree edge $e \in E(T)$ and a budget $b_f \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$ for each non-tree edge $f \in E(G) \setminus E(T)$. The goal is to find a maximum weight packing of fundamental cuts respecting the budgets. Equivalently, an instance of BPPT is an integer program of the form $\max \{w^\intercal x : Ax \le b,\ x \in \{0,1\}^n\}$ where $A \in \{0,1\}^{m \times n}$ is a transposed edge-path-tree matrix, $w \in \mathbb{Z}^n_{\ge 0}$ and $b \in \mathbb{Z}^m_{\ge 1}$. We define the congestion $C$ of a BPPT instance as the maximum number of non-zeros in a column of $A$. The unit congestion $UC$ is defined similarly, except that rows with $b_i \ge 2$ are ignored. We also consider the minimum budget $β:= \min \{b_i : i = 1, \ldots, m\}$. In this paper, we begin the study of BPPT through the lens of the three parameters $C$, $UC$ and $β$, and relative to the standard LP relaxation $\max \{w^\intercal x : Ax \le b,\ x \in [0,1]^n\}$. BPPT generalizes the independent set problem in graphs of maximum degree at most $C$ and is a special case of the $b$-matching problem in hypergraphs of rank at most $C$. We obtain approximation algorithms for BPPT with factors $2+UC/2$, $1+C/2$ and $β/(β-1)$ for $β\geq 2$. These bounds are relative to the standard LP relaxation and, as we show, integrality gap tight with respect to parameters $UC$ and $β$, and almost integrality gap tight relative to $C$. We complement these results with a $\lceil (C+1)/3 \rceil$-approximation for fixed $C$ which is not relative to the standard LP relaxation and has $\textsf{XP}$ running time parameterized by $C$.

items.title: Stochastic control representations for extremal solutions of HJB Dirichlet problems with measurable coefficients
items.summary: We study stochastic control problems for uniformly elliptic controlled diffusions on bounded domains whose coefficients are merely measurable in the state variable and whose drift is dominated by an $L_d$-function. The associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) Dirichlet problems may have more than one $L_p$-viscosity solution, so that the equation alone does not determine the value function. We show that the control problem selects the minimal solution: for all $p$ in a range $(d_0,d)$ determined by the spatial dimension, the ellipticity constant and the drift bound, the value function is the minimal $L_p$-viscosity supersolution of the HJB Dirichlet problem. In particular, every continuous $L_p$-viscosity supersolution bounds the optimal cost from above, which yields a one-sided verification theorem without regularity assumptions. We further prove the existence of optimal relaxed control rules for running costs dominated by an $L_p$-function, and the lower semicontinuity of the value function under perturbations of the coefficients. An example shows that upper semicontinuity may fail even when the coefficients are Lipschitz continuous in the control variable and the approximating coefficients are smooth, so that regularization may overestimate the optimal cost. The proof approximates arbitrary supersolutions from below by Sobolev supersolutions of HJB equations whose coefficients are modified only on sets of vanishing measure, and passes to the limit by means of Krylov estimates and martingale problem techniques.

items.title: Subexponential algorithms for structural parameterizations of Vertex Cover in geometric graphs
items.summary: A number of recent works have investigated the existence of parameterized subexponential algorithms in geometric graph classes for hitting a fixed small graph as a subgraph or as a minor. In this setting, given an $n$-vertex graph, the goal is to decide in time $n^{O(1)}2^{o(k)}$ if a solution of size at most $k$ exists. Inspired by recent results in kernelization for structural parameters, we investigate subexponential algorithms for the Vertex Cover (VC) problem, but parameterized by distance-to-triviality instead of solution size. More formally, given a fixed "trivial" graph class $\mathcal{C}$, the problem takes as input $(G,X,k)$, where $G \setminus X \in \mathcal{C}$, and asks if $G$ admits a vertex cover of size at most $k$. Our goal is to design algorithms for this problem running in time $n^{O(1)}2^{o(|X|)}$. The motivation is that, since $|X|$ is typically arbitrarily smaller than $k$, such algorithms might be faster than ETH-tight subexponential algorithms parameterized by $k$. We identify two sets of sufficient conditions under which the problem admits a subexponential algorithm: one for the case where $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of paths, and another for the case where $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of graphs of constant treedepth. We also provide two applications of these algorithmic results: we prove that $s$-string graphs and pseudo-disk graphs satisfy the first set of conditions, whereas string graphs satisfy the second set. The two sets share a common condition that might be of independent interest, as it implies a property that bounds the treewidth of any string graph in terms of a given modulator to a fixed graph class $\mathcal{C}$. Finally, concerning more restricted graph classes having the $ASQGM(ω)$ property (such as map graphs and $H$-minor free graphs), we prove a dichotomy, depending on the maximum treewidth in $\mathcal{C}$.

items.title: Finite-Step Algorithms for Input-Constrained Control Barrier Function-Based Safety Filters
items.summary: Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters commonly rely on quadratic programs (QPs) to modify nominal control inputs while satisfying safety constraints. For safety-critical applications, however, the solution must be computed reliably under actuator limitations and with predictable computational effort. General-purpose QP solvers typically rely on numerical convergence criteria, which do not directly provide finite bounds on algorithmic steps or distinguish solver failure from mathematical infeasibility. This paper considers CBF-QPs with a single affine safety constraint, componentwise input bounds, and diagonal quadratic weights. Exploiting the established scalar dual structure of continuous quadratic knapsack problems, we obtain a necessary and sufficient pointwise feasibility condition and an exact breakpoint-based solution procedure. The algorithm requires at most 2n positive breakpoint events for n inputs, reducing to at most n events when the nominal input is admissible. In the latter case, an exact saturation--redistribution algorithm computes the optimal solution in at most n passes. We further describe how the structured solution can be combined with verified floating-point constraint evaluation to distinguish certified feasible commands, certified infeasibility, and unresolved numerical cases. The resulting framework provides an exact and computationally predictable solution procedure for a practically relevant class of input-constrained CBF safety filters.

items.title: A Deterministic Algorithm for Eigenvalue Separation in Tridiagonal Matrices
items.summary: We develop a deterministic algorithm for separating the eigenvalues of Hermitian tridiagonal matrices by small diagonal perturbations. For $\|T\|_2\leq1$, $0<δ<1/2$, and $X=\mathrm{diag}(1,\ldots,n)$, our algorithm selects $t\in[0,δ/n]$ such that $D=tX$ satisfies $\|D\|_2\leqδ$ and $\mathrm{gap}(T+D)>c\,δ^2n^{-12}$ for an absolute constant $c>0$. The construction uses a classical convex weighted eigenvalue sum and its finite-scale slope variation. A tridiagonal localization argument turns near-degenerate eigenvalues into separated responses to the fixed diagonal direction, yielding a quantitative gap certificate. An adaptive interval selector then identifies a certifying window in at most $\lceil\log_2(16n^3)\rceil$ refinements, using $O(\log n)$ evaluations of the weighted eigenvalue sum to inverse-polynomial accuracy. A structure-exploiting implementation uses rigorous Sturm eigenvalue enclosures and adaptive precision to certify the stopping condition on six families of test matrices. The directly certified gaps are substantially larger than the worst-case analytical bounds, illustrating both the effectiveness of the construction and the conservatism of the universal certificate. Our results give a deterministic answer to the eigenvalue-separation question underlying the deterministic Minami perturbation problem for tridiagonal matrices.

items.title: Fast HOSVD via Randomized Preconditioning and Mixed Precision
items.summary: Computing dominant mode subspaces is a major cost in the higher-order singular value decomposition (HOSVD) and its sequentially truncated variant (STHOSVD). Randomized Tucker algorithms can reduce this cost by approximating the required subspaces from small sketches, but may introduce additional approximation errors. We exploit the extreme aspect ratios of tensor unfoldings, whose mode dimensions can remain manageable while being orders of magnitude smaller than the products of the remaining dimensions. Instead of directly approximating the desired subspaces, we sketch the entire unfolding at a scale comparable to its mode dimension to preserve its full row-space geometry, and use randomized preconditioning to recover the desired singular subspaces through small matrix factorizations. We develop randomized preconditioned HOSVD and STHOSVD algorithms incorporating numerical truncation, and further accelerate their large matrix multiplications using mixed precision. Our analysis shows that truncation adds only a term quadratic in the numerical threshold to the classical HOSVD tail-energy bound, while mixed precision introduces a relative \(O(\sqrt{u_\ell})\) correction to the tail-energy term and an additive \(O(u_\ell)\) term under suitable conditions, where \(u_\ell\) is the lower-precision unit roundoff. On synthetic and real tensors, our methods achieve speedups of a fewfold to several dozenfold over classical HOSVD and STHOSVD, with runtimes competitive with those of other randomized methods. The double-precision versions match the classical reconstruction errors to numerical precision, and the mixed-precision variants yield nearly identical errors.

items.title: Nonlinear Joint State and Noise Estimation under Packet Dropouts and Additive Measurement Corruption
items.summary: This paper investigates joint state and noise covariance estimation for nonlinear systems subject to dual reliability impairments: random packet dropouts and additive measurement corruption. This scenario poses challenging nonconjugate inference, as clean and corrupted measurements share an unknown baseline covariance $\boldsymbol{R}_k$ with fixed known corruption covariance $\boldsymbol{E}_k$. Packet reception is observable, whereas the authenticity of received measurements remains latent and must be inferred. To resolve this intractable estimation problem, we cast joint posterior inference as a variational optimization problem and develop a conjugate variational inference adaptive Kalman filter with dual reliability (CVIAKF-DR). The proposed method retains analytical updates for the prediction covariance and two reliability probabilities, while adopting CVI to estimate the state and baseline measurement covariance. The covariance update combines the analytical contribution from clean measurements with Monte Carlo gradient estimates for corrupted measurements. Numerical results on a re-entry tracking benchmark demonstrate the superior accuracy of the proposed method in both state and noise covariance estimation. Remarkably, even built upon the linear Kalman filtering (KF) framework that is originally designed for linear systems, our method achieves more accurate estimation performance than dedicated nonlinear filtering algorithms based on the cubature Kalman filter (CKF).

items.title: Learning Morse Lyapunov functions through invertible neural networks
items.summary: Towards data-driven stability certificates of dynamical systems, we are witnessing renewed interest in studying and exploiting the structure of Lyapunov functions. Especially Lyapunov functions that are locally quadratic (i.e., Morse) gained popularity ever since it was understood that they can be written as the norm squared of a diffeomorphism. This topological representation alludes to parametrizations using invertible neural networks. In this note we discuss when and how such functions can be learned. In particular, using neural ODEs (NODEs), we characterize Sobolev approximation of these diffeomorphisms on compact sets and show how this naturally relates to stability. We also connect our results to PLNets and supply numerical experiments for illustration.

items.title: The Exact Optimal Delivery Scheme for the Cyclically $L$-Separated Placement in Multi-Access Coded Caching
items.summary: This paper investigates the $(K, L, M, N)$ multi-access coded caching (MACC) system introduced by Hachem et al. The system consists of a server storing $N$ equal-sized files, $K$ cache nodes, each with a storage capacity of $M$ files, and $K$ users, each accessing $L$ consecutive cache nodes in a cyclic wrap-around topology. The server transmits coded information to the users via an error-free capacitated broadcast channel, such that each user obtains its own requested file as a combination of the server transmission and the accessible caches' content. Our objective is to minimize the worst-case transmission load over all possible user demands. First, for the cyclically $L$-separated placement, we derive a new converse bound using the acyclic index coding bound. By carefully counting all valid cache supports, the proposed converse improves upon an existing bound for the same placement. We then develop a linear coded caching scheme based on a novel determinant-based interference alignment strategy, which achieves the new converse bound exactly. Exploiting the determinant structure of a random generating matrix (each of whose columns corresponds to one user), this scheme simultaneously aligns interference across all users into low-dimensional subspaces, while preserving the decodability of their desired packets. Furthermore, by averaging acyclic index coding bounds over cyclic user permutations, we derive a general converse bound applicable to arbitrary uncoded cache placements. By combining the proposed scheme with memory sharing, we demonstrate that the achievable transmission load is within a factor of two of the global bound under uncoded placement. Finally, theoretical and numerical comparisons demonstrate that the proposed scheme generally achieves a strictly lower load than existing schemes.

items.title: Optimal Quadrature and the Curse of Dimensionality for a Veronese Class
items.summary: We study integration on a $3^d$-dimensional trigonometric space whose unit ball has all coordinate mixed partial derivatives bounded by one. With evaluations anywhere in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we determine the exact minimal worst-case error among all deterministic algorithms using at most $n$ function values. An optimal quadrature formula is obtained by truncating an exact product quadrature formula on $\{1/2, 1/2+π\}^d$. All weights are positive. For each error tolerance $0<\varepsilon<1$, the information complexity grows exponentially in $d$ with the common base $Λ\approx 1.10546546$. The correction of order $\sqrt{d}$ to the logarithm of the information complexity and the corresponding error limit are determined by the standard normal distribution function. For $b\ge 1$ and $n=\lceil b^d\rceil$, the error tends to one, one half, or zero according as $b<Λ$, $b=Λ$, or $b>Λ$.

items.title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
items.summary: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

items.title: A Rollout-Based Approach to Real-Time Topology and Dispatch Control in the AI4RealNet L2RPN Benchmark
items.summary: Operating transmission networks under uncertain outages requires coordinating discrete network topology actions with continuous adjustments to generation and storage, while respecting operational constraints and real-time computational limits. We present a rollout-based controller that combines discrete and continuous decisions under the uncertain contingency policy of the L2RPN AI4RealNet 2026 challenge. Power-flow approximations and convex optimization identify the most promising actions, followed by short-horizon simulations to predict their effect on congestion, renewable curtailment, and redispatching costs. A further policy exploits the benchmark's specific attack protocol: keeping selected lines disconnected prevents some adversarial outages from being initiated. On the benchmark's $118$-bus network, the controller completed $189$ of $208$ final-test scenarios (score $64.39$) and achieved the second-best ratio of score to computation time among the five top-ranked entries, behind one that scored lower. Our results show that combining structured optimization with simulation-based action selection is effective even without a learned decision rule, and fast enough for real-time control. Code and reproduction material: https://github.com/DavidKrame/RAD_agent__AI4RealNet_competition.

items.title: Copying along Arithmetic Progressions Cannot Simulate Interleaving with Polylogarithmic Loss
items.summary: Two classical ways to compress a word are straight-line programs (SLPs), which build it by concatenating smaller pieces, and the Lempel-Ziv 77 (LZ77) factorisation, which copies earlier parts of it; their sizes are measures of repetitiveness. LZ77 approximates the smallest SLP efficiently: it has no more factors than a smallest SLP has size, and yields an SLP at most a logarithmic factor larger in near-linear time. Motivated by online prediction, Kosoy introduced zipline programs, which are analogous to SLPs but interleave their pieces round-robin instead of concatenating them. Her generalisation of LZ77, the arithmetic repetition system, describes a word by copies from one arithmetic progression of positions to a later one. Do arithmetic repetition systems approximate the smallest zipline program as well? Kosoy proved that the least size $\mathrm{ARC}(x)$ of an arithmetic repetition system for a word $x$ of length $n$ is at most a factor $O(n^{1/3})$ larger than the least size $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ of a zipline program for it, and asked whether this factor is tight. Her polynomial-time next-letter predictor makes $O(\mathrm{ARC}(x)\log n)$ mistakes, so a polylogarithmic factor would bound its mistakes by $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, which no known polynomial-time predictor achieves. We show that the optimal exponent is $1/4$, not $1/3$: $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \le 2n^{1/4}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ for every word $x$, and at every large enough length $n$ some binary word has $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \ge n^{1/4-o(1)}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$.

items.title: Branch-and-Cut for Maximum $k$-Independent Sets with Spectral Bounds
items.summary: We develop a branch-and-cut method for finding maximum distance-independent sets in graphs. Our approach solves a sequence of fixed-size clique problems, combining graph reductions with combinatorial and spectral bounds. We give a compact formulation, derive strengthened inequalities, establish conditions for using spectral information, and evaluate them in a comprehensive computational study.

items.title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs
items.summary: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of RFM remain incompletely elucidated. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of RFM within the framework of kernel methods, focusing on two principal aspects: (i) approximation by finitely many random features in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm, and (ii) estimation over the induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) from finitely many noiseless collocation observations. We relate both problems to kernel ridge regression (KRR) and establish upper and lower bounds in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operators under the respective assumptions. Combining the approximation and estimation lower bounds, we establish a lower bound under simultaneous restrictions on the numbers of random features and collocation observations. We further quantify how activation regularity affects these eigenvalues, obtaining algebraic upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential upper bounds for analytic activations.

items.title: Convergence rates of moment--SOS hierarchies with correlative sparsity via gluing and projection
items.summary: This paper studies convergence rates of moment--SOS hierarchies with correlative sparsity. Following the method proposed in~\cite{tran}, we bound the Hausdorff distance between the set of sparse truncated moment sequences and sparse truncated pseudo-moment sequences. The central step is a quantitative gluing lemma on a clique tree: local moment errors and separator discrepancies in total variation control the error of a joint approximating measure. Over hypercube, polynomial kernels give the convergence rates $O((\log_2r)^3/r^2)$ for the correlative sparse quadratic module and $O(r^{-2})$ for the correlative sparse preordering, where the certificate degree is $2r$. On compact basic semialgebraic sets, slack variable lifting and global atom projection yield $O((\log_2r)^{3\Lo/2}/r^{\Lo})$ and $O(r^{-\Lo})$ with a Łojasiewicz exponent $0<\Lo \le1$. These bounds hold for fixed-degree Hausdorff distances and polynomial objective gaps. We also extend to result to the correlative sparse quadratic-module rate for scalar objectives with clique-local polynomial matrix constraints.

items.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
items.summary: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

items.title: Analysis and Design of Spatially Coupled LDPC Codes for Pulsed-Jamming-Resilient Space Telemetry
items.summary: Jamming is a major threat to space telemetry downlinks, which operate under severe power and bandwidth constraints. This paper develops a jamming-aware analysis and design framework for protograph-based spatially coupled low-density parity-check (SC-LDPC) codes. For pulsed jamming with jamming state information (JSI) at the receiver, we derive a two-state protograph-based extrinsic information transfer (PEXIT) recursion that tracks the messages originating from clean and jammed symbols separately and merges them at the check nodes through a mutual-information-matched Gaussian approximation. For non-interleaved pulsed jamming, we map each pulse realization, through the serialization of the lifted codeword, to a profile of jammed fractions over the variable-node types, and we prove that, under random lifting, this profile determines the local channel-state statistics. The resulting position-dependent thresholds are the objective of a constrained differential-evolution search over protographs, coupling memories, and edge spreadings. At different code rates, the designed ensembles are compared with the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) accumulate, repeat-by-4, and jagged accumulate (AR4JA) LDPC codes whose block length matches the SC-LDPC constraint length, with longer AR4JA codes whose block length is comparable with the size of the sliding window decoder, and with non-optimized SC-LDPC codes. Under pulsed jamming with random pulse positions and with JSI, the ensembles designed over random pulse realizations, decoded through sliding window decoding, reach a bit error rate of $10^{-4}$ at lower signal-to-noise ratios than all the benchmarks.

items.title: Quantitative approximation for Fourier neural operators in controlled ordinary differential equations
items.summary: Fourier neural operators (FNOs) avoid the curse of parametric complexity when approximating the solution operator of certain partial differential equations (PDEs). While recent studies primarily focus on PDEs, in this article we derive upper error bounds for approximating the solution operator of controlled ordinary differential equations (CODEs) $\dot{y}=f(y,u)$ using a FNO. Under a Carathéodory setting and suitable regularity assumptions, including a smallness condition, we prove that the size of the FNO grows at most algebraically in $1/\varepsilon$, namely like $\varepsilon^{-(1+d/(2(s-1)))}$ up to logarithmic factors for GELU networks, and is thus sub-quadratic for sufficiently smooth $f$, where $d=1+n_y+n_u$ and $s$ denotes the Sobolev regularity of $f$. Our proof is based on emulating the Picard iteration through the layers of the FNO while exploiting the differentiation formula of the discrete Fourier transform. This result contributes to the quantitative approximation theory of FNOs for physically motivated problems and provides a theoretical foundation for leveraging a FNO as efficient forward surrogate for the solution operator of CODEs, especially in inverse parameter estimation where repeated evaluations of the forward operator are needed.

items.title: Positive Regulation of an Axial Dispersion Tubular Reactor by Optimal Boundary Feedback Control
items.summary: The dynamics of the reactant in an isothermal axial dispersion tubular reactor is considered. Our goal consists in designing the inlet reactant concentration, under the form of a state feedback law, in order to modify the state behavior according to relevant process requirements, while keeping the positivity and stability properties of the uncontrolled dynamics. The designed control is also constrained to be positive to respect physical requirements. First, we state and analytically solve a parameterized optimal feedback design problem. Next, we address a positive observer-based feedback stabilization problem. The results are illustrated by means of numerical simulations.

items.title: Practical Semantic Communication for General-Purpose Networks: Compression of High-Dimensional Embeddings Under Quantization
items.summary: This paper introduces a practical framework for semantic communication over wireless channels, focusing on the compression of high-dimensional embeddings under quantization and channel errors. Building upon a relaxed Gaussian Information Bottleneck (GIB) model, the approach provides analytical solutions for task-relevant information preservation, even with non-Gaussian targets. The framework relaxes traditional Gaussian assumptions, enabling effective compression for discrete and complex data such as text embeddings. It derives closed-form gradients for optimizing the compression matrix and establishes bounds linking continuous representations to discrete, noisy system performance. Comprehensive experiments on text classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms task-agnostic quantization-based compression methods, maintaining high semantic fidelity at low bit budgets per embedding. The approach offers a scalable, interpretable, and resource-efficient solution for deploying semantic communication in general-purpose networks.

items.title: Unconditionally Positive Nonstandard Finite Difference Schemes for $p$-Laplacian Reaction--Diffusion Equations
items.summary: We propose a conservative, semi-implicit nonstandard finite difference scheme for the reaction--diffusion equation $u_t=λ(|u_x|^{p-2}u_x)_x+f(u)$, $p>1$, where, as is customary, the $p$-Laplacian is regularized by a parameter $\eps>0$. The scheme combines a denominator function, a lagged diffusion coefficient, and a nonlocal treatment of the loss part of the reaction. For every time step and mesh size we prove that the scheme is well posed and positive, that it preserves an invariant region $[0,K]$ whenever the reaction admits one, and that it reproduces every constant equilibrium exactly. Without reaction, it conserves mass, satisfies a discrete maximum principle, and, for $1<p\le 2$, decreases a discrete energy. An example shows that the energy may increase for $p>2$. The truncation error is $O(k+h^2)$ at interior nodes. Numerical tests confirm first order in time and second order in space, and show that the scheme remains positive and bounded for step sizes at which the explicit method breaks down.

items.title: Maximum principle preserving approximation of scalar conservation equations with a fractional Laplacian
items.summary: In this paper, we propose a maximum principle preserving continuous finite element method for scalar conservation laws augmented with a fractional diffusion operator of order $s\in (0,1)$. Conservation laws with fractional diffusion operators arise in a variety of physical models involving anomalous transport and nonlocal regularization, including geophysical flows, plasma physics, and nonlinear acoustics. The fractional Laplacian is approximated using a sinc-quadrature representation, yielding a resolvent-based formulation compatible with continuous finite elements and explicit strong stability preserving Runge--Kutta time integration. A first-order monotone scheme is constructed using graph viscosity and is shown to satisfy a discrete maximum principle under an explicit CFL condition. A high-order extension is obtained via entropy-consistent corrections and convex limiting, achieving second-order accuracy while preserving the maximum principle, and hence positivity, as well as mass conservation in the periodic setting. Numerical experiments, including applications to the Surface Quasi-Geostrophic equation, confirm the second-order accuracy and the robustness of the proposed method on unstructured meshes.

items.title: Optimal Importance Sampling Densities for Estimating Several Expectations at Once
items.summary: Simulation studies often estimate several quantities from a single sample, and the best importance sampling density depends on how the errors on these quantities are combined. We characterise the optimal auxiliary density for a general error criterion. We show that it is the nominal density reweighted by a weighted length of the vector of estimated functions, where the weights are set by the error criterion, or by the curvature of the loss when the criterion comes from a loss on the errors. We also provide a lower bound on the best achievable error. The optimal density is explicit for smooth losses, including the usual losses on covariance matrices. We also derive allocation laws for the cells of a histogram and characterise the minimax density for the probabilities of several events. When there is no closed form, we show how to compute the optimal density numerically.

items.title: A conic optimization framework for shape-constrained functional regression analysis
items.summary: Standard regression methods do not always guarantee that the estimated model reflects prior knowledge about how predictors relate to the response, which motivates constrained regression. When the effects to be estimated are smooth nonlinear functions, a natural family of constraints is that of shape constraints, such as sign, monotonicity, or curvature, which encode qualitative properties that these functions are often expected to satisfy. While shape-constrained estimation of smooth functions is well established in classical regression with scalar covariates and response, its extension to functional regression, where the coefficients are themselves functions, remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose the functional shape-constrained conic P-spline estimator (FunSCOPE), a unified framework for shape-constrained functional linear regression that covers scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and function-on-function models, and in which any combination of the shapes above can be imposed on the functional regression coefficient. Building on a P-spline approach, the desired shapes are expressed as conditions on the scalar regression coefficients, which leads to an estimation problem formulated as a conic optimization problem. For univariate coefficients, as in scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and a particular case of the function-on-function regression, the concurrent case, these conditions are both necessary and sufficient, in contrast to existing approaches, which provide only sufficient conditions; for bivariate coefficients, as in general function-on-function models, they are neither necessary nor sufficient. Numerical experiments show that FunSCOPE outperforms competing methods in terms of estimation error and computational time.

items.title: Network-Native DNN Architecture Synthesis for Distributed Inference
items.summary: Distributed deep neural network (DNN) inference typically follows a model-first paradigm, in which a predefined DNN is partitioned and deployed over a physical network. On irregular communication-computation topologies, however, this approach can create transmission bottlenecks and leave distributed resources underutilized. This paper reverses this perspective and asks: given a physical network, what kind of DNN can it naturally support? To answer this question, we propose a network-native DNN architecture synthesis paradigm in which the physical network topology directly defines inter-node neural dependencies. Neural computation is allocated across nodes under communication, computation, storage, synchronization, and latency constraints. We establish structural properties of the synthesis problem and develop linear programming (LP)-based Architecture Synthesis (LPAS), an efficient topology-guided algorithm that produces a feasible architecture with a computable bound on suboptimality. Experiments on physical networks of different sizes show that LPAS achieves relative gaps below 0.6% to the LP-derived upper bound, with substantially lower runtime than direct mixed-integer LP optimization on larger networks. Under matched network deadlines, the network-native architectures activate more compute nodes and utilize a larger proportion of available model-storage capacity than the model-first baseline. After training, the network-native models achieve higher classification accuracy across all evaluated dataset-precision settings, with the average gain of up to 10.69%. This network-native design paradigm thus turns the physical network from a deployment constraint into an architecture design primitive.

items.title: High-order Crank-Nicolson method via diagonal Padé factorization
items.summary: We present a numerical method to solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation at arbitrary order of accuracy in the time step, particularly well suited for tridiagonal Hamilton operators. The method is based on a factorization of the diagonal Padé approximants of the matrix exponential into products of linear factors, which preserves tridiagonal matrix structure at every time step and yields a propagator of order 2q in the time step at a cost of O(qN) operations. The propagator is exactly unitary by construction, and at lowest order q=1 it reduces to the standard Crank-Nicolson algorithm. We further extend the method to any Hamiltonian admitting a decomposition into a sum of tridiagonal or diagonal operators via high-order split-operator techniques (McLachlan, 2022), retaining O(qN) scaling at each time step. We also analytically show and numerically verify that the precision is dictated by the split-operator method. This covers a broad range of physically relevant cases, including higher-dimensional systems, higher-order spatial discretizations, and non-separable potentials.

items.title: Sign Primal-Dual Gradient Dynamics for Supply-Demand Coordination under Binary Human Feedback
items.summary: This paper addresses supply-demand coordination, in which a supplier sets prices to balance the demands of multiple buyers against limited resources. Existing studies typically solve the supply-demand coordination problem with a distributed algorithm called primal-dual gradient dynamics (PDGD), assuming that each buyer discloses the value of its own utility or marginal utility function. In contrast, we assume that each buyer discloses only binary information, namely whether it wants more or less of the current amount, and propose Sign PDGD. Sign PDGD is a PDGD algorithm in which the buyers' update depends only on the sign information. We analyze the convergence of Sign PDGD by interpreting it as a sliding mode control (SMC). For a quadratic cost and linear constraints, we show that under a gain condition, the primal and dual variables converge to the optimal solution. Numerical simulations on a toy resource-sharing problem confirm the two-phase behavior of SMC and show that the primal and dual variables approach the optimal solution.

items.title: Speed-Robust Scheduling for Total Completion Time
items.summary: We study two-stage speed-robust scheduling for minimizing total completion time. Jobs must be partitioned into $M$ bags before an adversary reveals the speeds of at most $M$ machines. Each bag is then assigned to one available machine, and the jobs on each machine may be processed in any order independent of the bags. We compare with an optimal schedule that knows the speeds in advance and assigns jobs individually. This model has been studied for makespan minimization. We initiate its study for total completion time, as suggested by Stein and Zhong (TALG 2020). For an unknown number of identical machines, we show that the optimal deterministic robustness factor is exactly~$13/12$, both for unit-size jobs and for arbitrary processing times. For infinitesimally small jobs, the factor lies between $31/30\approx1.0333$ and $28/27\approx1.0370$, well below the optimal makespan factor of about $1.2071$. General speeds make the problem strictly harder: no deterministic algorithm is better than $1.2669$-robust, already for infinitesimally small jobs. We give a $25/16$-robust algorithm for arbitrary processing times and improve the guarantee to $1681/1152\approx1.4592$ for infinitesimally small jobs. Our main tools are a layer decomposition that extends guarantees from unit-size jobs to arbitrary processing times when one assignment satisfies them for every prefix in non-increasing processing-time order, and a threshold analysis of the bag counts produced by greedy assignment rules.

items.title: A Lifted Hessian-Riemannian Gradient Flow for LQR Synthesis under Passivity Constraints
items.summary: The static state-feedback gain that renders a linear system passive at an external port and minimizes a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) cost cannot be computed by convex optimization, since the passivity certificate and the LQR cost are coupled bilinearly through the common gain. A previous indirect approach restricts the gain to a convex inner approximation of the passivity region, which is conservative and whose construction scales exponentially with the number of gain entries. This paper proposes a direct approach. The set of strictly passivating gains is the image of a convex lifted set of inverse storage matrices and transformed gains. We describe this set by a strict linear matrix inequality and an affine equality for every feedthrough matrix with positive semidefinite symmetric part, including feedthrough matrices with a singular symmetric part, and minimize the LQR cost over it by a gradient flow whose metric is the Hessian of a logarithmic barrier. For multi-input systems, this Hessian is singular along gain changes that preserve the storage function, and we complete the metric along these directions by the metric of the gain space. We prove that the flow exists for all times, that every gain along the flow is strictly passivating with an explicit storage function, and that the cost decreases monotonically while the gains remain in a compact set of stabilizing gains. Numerical examples show that the flow attains a lower cost than the indirect approach, that the completion is required for multi-input systems, and that the flow can converge to a local minimizer on nonconvex passivity regions.

items.title: An adaptive Gaussian splitting scheme for linear Fokker--Planck equations
items.summary: We develop an adaptive numerical method for linear Fokker--Planck equations on $\mathbb R^d$, based on approximating the evolving probability density by linear combinations of Gaussian functions (LCGs). The method applies to polynomial-type drift fields, without requiring a gradient-flow structure or a stationary distribution.
